analysis.one_liner: Overrides state laws that block cities, towns, and co-ops from offering broadband service.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Roughly a dozen states have laws that bar or restrict cities, towns, and electric co-ops from building their own internet networks. This bill would amend the Telecommunications Act of 1996 to say no state may stop a public provider, a public-private partnership, or a cooperative from offering broadband [S3]. It also requires those public providers to apply their local rules to competing private companies without favoring themselves [S2]. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities where private broadband companies have declined to build fast, affordable service, because their city or local co-op could finally offer a competing option. Rural areas served by electric co-ops would be a prime example, since co-ops already have poles, trenches, and utility customers.

how_it_helps.text: Removes state-level bans that currently prohibit public providers, public-private partnerships, and cooperatively organized providers from offering advanced telecommunications service [S3].

Includes a savings clause keeping public networks subject to the same federal and state rules as every other provider, and an antidiscrimination requirement so a city cannot tilt its own regulations in favor of its network over private competitors [S3].
Defines 'state or local entity' to include Indian Tribes, so tribal governments could also build broadband under the bill [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable and telephone companies would face new competition in towns and counties where they are currently shielded by state law. State governments would lose the authority to ban municipal networks. Where a city finances a network with bonds, local taxpayers would bear the risk if the network underperforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable and phone incumbents; some local taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Municipal networks can be expensive to build and slow to reach break-even; if a city-funded network fails or underperforms, local taxpayers, not private shareholders, would be on the hook for the debt [S3].

Critics argue government-run providers can have unfair advantages (tax-exempt financing, rights-of-way, access to utility customers) that private competitors cannot match; the bill's antidiscrimination clause addresses regulatory favoritism but does not equalize those structural advantages [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the many communities that private providers have not served well, the potential upside is real: a locally accountable competitor with no shareholder margin. The genuine risks are that city-owned networks can misprice or over-borrow, and taxpayers would absorb those losses. The bill's antidiscrimination and savings clauses address the most serious fair-competition objections, but the taxpaying risk of failed public networks remains the honest cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 19, 2023 by Sen. Booker with five original cosponsors (3 Democrats, 2 Independents) and read twice on the floor [S1].
The same day it was referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; that referral was the last action on the bill in the 118th Congress [S5].
The committee held no markup and the Senate never debated or voted on the bill; the CRS summary was never updated beyond the introduced version [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies are better off because the bill died: state laws that keep municipal and co-op networks out of their markets remain in force. Communities still waiting for a public broadband option gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let state and local governments, partnerships, and co-ops offer broadband despite state bans [S1].

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, King, Markey, Sanders, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none were Republicans [S4].

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no hearing, no floor report [S5].

against.name: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies and their state lobbying arms
against.what_they_did: Backed and benefit from the state laws banning or restricting municipal broadband that this bill would have overturned; the bill faced no recorded floor opposition because it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to reveal a broader partisan split [S4].

industries.note: State bans on municipal and co-op networks shield these companies from competition in areas they have chosen not to serve or underserve. The bill would have removed that shield, exposing them to public and co-op competitors.
These entities already own poles, trenches, and billing relationships that make broadband networks cheaper to build. The bill would let them enter broadband wherever state law currently forbids it.
The bill expressly defines tribes and local governments as eligible public providers, restoring an option state statutes had taken away.
